challenges.headline: Building before checking existing tools
challenges.premise: The request says 'we need an app', taking a custom build as given.
challenges.alternative: If the registration or ticketing platform already in use has a check-in feature, or a bought check-in app covers the need, switching it on or buying it could replace most of the build. A custom build then only covers the gaps.
challenges.consequence: Building something that already exists, or is already paid for, spends the budget and the limited time before a fixed date on a solved problem.
challenges.recommendation: Before any design, find out what registration tool supplies the list, whether it has check-in, and what budget exists. Build only the gap between that and the need.

challenges.headline: Assumed good connectivity
challenges.premise: The request reads as if scanning and recording simply work at the entrance.
challenges.alternative: Treat offline operation as a decision to make explicitly. Either the venue connectivity is verified, or the devices hold a local copy of the list and sync check-ins later.
challenges.consequence: Offline and online-only are different architectures. Discovering the venue has a weak signal late means a rebuild, or a queue at the door in front of the client.
challenges.recommendation: Ask about venue connectivity now and, if possible, test it on site. Decide online-only or offline-capable before estimating.

challenges.headline: Check-in as a single event
challenges.premise: Checking in is treated as one simple act per person.
challenges.alternative: Define the cases separately: first entry, a repeat scan that is a duplicate, re-entry after stepping out, and entry to a different zone or session. The simplest option is one check-in per person with a clear warning on repeat scans.
challenges.consequence: Without a decision, the data model may not support what the client later wants, such as per-zone attendance, and two devices may disagree on the same person.
challenges.recommendation: Get the client to choose the meaning of a second scan and write down what the app does for each case.

briefs.problem: Staff at the venue entrance need a fast, reliable way to identify arriving attendees and record their arrival on a fixed event day. The underlying driver (queues, headcount, access control, or an attendance deliverable) was not stated and is assumed.
briefs.solution: A staff-facing check-in app that holds the attendee list on the device, identifies people by scan or name search, records arrival, and handles people not on the list, with a live count and attendance record afterwards (assumed, not yet requested).
introduces: an attendee list held on staff devices, with a defined freshness and sync model
a check-in event record that can hold duplicate, re-entry and per-zone arrivals
a manual fallback path: fuzzy name search and on-the-spot registration for walk-ins
a multi-device rule for the same person processed at two entrances within seconds
an attendance record and export that serves as a post-event deliverable

challenges.headline: Build versus buy
challenges.premise: A custom app is needed for entrance check-in.
challenges.alternative: If the attendee list already sits in a registration or ticketing tool, that tool's check-in feature or an off-the-shelf event check-in app may cover scanning, name search, walk-ins and a live count. That would replace the build with configuration plus a rehearsal.
challenges.consequence: Building a door app that duplicates a feature already licensed spends a fixed, immovable timeline on offline sync, concurrency and fallbacks that a mature product has already solved. The request names no tool and no reason an existing one was ruled out, so this has not been tested.
challenges.recommendation: Before any design work, list the registration tools in use and the off-the-shelf check-in options considered, and record why each was rejected. Build only against a concrete gap, such as a custom rule, a required integration or a budget limit.

challenges.headline: Assuming the venue is online
challenges.premise: Staff will have a working connection at the entrance, so the app can run online-only.
challenges.alternative: Treat offline operation as a decision to be made explicitly. An offline-capable app holds a snapshot of the list and syncs check-ins later. An online-only app is simpler, but the door stops if the network drops. A middle path is a snapshot loaded before doors open, with check-ins queued and synced when possible.
challenges.consequence: Online-only is cheaper to build and fails in front of the client on a day that cannot be rescheduled. Offline-capable is a different architecture, with conflict rules, a visible pending state and stale-list risk, and it cannot be bolted on late.
challenges.recommendation: Ask for the venue's real connectivity at the entrances and settle online-only versus offline before estimating. If connectivity is unknown, plan for the snapshot-plus-sync model and test it at the venue.

challenges.headline: What "check in" means
challenges.premise: Check-in is a single arrival per attendee.
challenges.alternative: Decide up front whether a second scan is a duplicate to block, a re-entry to allow, or an arrival at a different zone or session to record separately. A simple one-arrival version can be shipped first if that is genuinely all that is needed.
challenges.consequence: The three meanings need different data models. Choosing a single-arrival flag and discovering later that zones or re-entry matter means reworking the data model and the exports built on it.
challenges.recommendation: Get the client to state the rule for a repeat scan and whether zones or sessions exist, and record it as the first business rule.

briefs.solution: A staff-facing check-in app for the entrance that identifies an attendee by scan or name search, records arrival, and gives a manual fallback when identification fails. Zones, offline use and reuse are not yet decided.

challenges.headline: Building rather than buying
challenges.premise: A custom app is needed for door check-in.
challenges.alternative: Ready-made check-in tools exist, and the registration platform, if there is one, may already include a check-in feature that is paid for but not switched on. Using one of these could cover the core scan-and-record loop with no build. The request does not say whether either was looked at.
challenges.consequence: If an existing tool covers the need, a custom build spends money and rehearsal time on a door-critical path that someone else has already hardened. If none fits, the reasons for rejecting them become the real requirements.
challenges.recommendation: Before any design, check the registration platform for a check-in feature and shortlist two or three off-the-shelf tools. Record exactly what each fails to do (offline use, categories, export format) and build only that gap.

challenges.headline: Online-only door assumption
challenges.premise: Staff scan at the entrance as if the venue network will be reliable all day.
challenges.alternative: Decide offline behaviour explicitly. Either the devices hold a local copy of the attendee list and sync check-ins later, or the build commits to online-only with a manual paper fallback. This is a choice about architecture, not a setting added late.
challenges.consequence: Venue entrances can have weak or saturated signal. An online-only build then fails at the peak, in front of the client, and the offline sync layer, which is where correctness problems concentrate, would have to be retrofitted close to a fixed date.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the venue or test signal at the actual doors, then choose offline-capable or online-only before estimating. If offline, define how fresh the local list must be and how conflicts between devices resolve.

challenges.headline: Check-in as a single event
challenges.premise: Checking in means recording one arrival per person.
challenges.alternative: Define a second scan explicitly: refuse it as a duplicate, allow it as re-entry, or record it as access to a different zone or session. Each needs a different data model, and the request does not say which applies.
challenges.consequence: A one-arrival model must be reworked if zones or re-entry turn up later, and with several doors the same person scanned twice within seconds becomes an undefined outcome.
challenges.recommendation: Settle the meaning of a second scan and whether any zones or sessions exist before modelling check-in. If the answer is unclear, start with entrance-only check-in and a defined duplicate warning.

complexity_reasons: an unknown offline versus online choice that changes the architecture
an attendee list that keeps changing, with an on-site path for walk-ins and substitutions
peak throughput measured on the actual devices
briefs.cost_driver: the offline and sync decision combined with multi-door concurrency
risks: Failure at the door in front of the client on an immovable date, with no second attempt. Every automated path needs a manual fallback.
Weak venue connectivity may only be discovered on site, after the architecture has been fixed.
Attendee personal data (GDPR) sits on staff devices and in exports. Retention after the event and what sponsors may receive are unspecified.
The operators are untrained staff seeing the app for the first time that morning, so anything that needs explanation will slow the queue.
The attendee list source is unknown, so the effort for import versus live integration could change substantially once it is identified.

opportunities.text: Keep the check-in flow, attendee and category model and offline/sync layer separate from event-specific branding, zones and export format, so a second event is configuration rather than a rebuild. Worth deciding only once the client confirms there will be more events.
Treat the check-in records as the source for the live headcount and the post-event attendance export, so one accurate dataset serves the door, the dashboard and the client deliverable.

next_steps: Run the build-or-buy check first: look at the registration platform's check-in feature and shortlist off-the-shelf tools, and stop here if one covers the need.

In the same conversation, confirm where the attendee list comes from, how it changes up to the event, the expected attendee count, number of doors and devices, and the target seconds per person at peak.
Check signal at the actual entrances and decide offline-capable versus online-only, and what a second scan means.
Agree acceptance scenarios for the door (QR failure, name not on the list, duplicate scan, two doors at once) and book a rehearsal on real devices in the venue before the date.

decisions.decision: The event date is fixed and cannot move, so scope is cut against it and a venue rehearsal is part of the scope
decisions.why: A failed check-in on the day has no recovery, so reliability is worth more than extra features.
decisions.alternative: Plan for a later fix after launch.
decisions.tradeoff: Fewer features in exchange for a rehearsed, conservative check-in path.

decisions.decision: Every scan path has a manual fallback (name search, on-the-spot registration)
decisions.why: Scanning will fail for some arrivals in real conditions, and a stuck queue is the visible failure.
decisions.tradeoff: More to build and rehearse, in exchange for not blocking the door when a scan fails.

decisions.decision: The app is for door staff, who are a known set of users reached through rollout rather than acquisition

open_decisions: Build, buy or switch on an existing check-in feature, and the budget
Source and update pattern of the attendee list, including walk-ins and substitutions
Offline-capable or online-only
Meaning of a second scan, and whether zones or sessions exist
Expected attendee volume, number of doors and devices, and target seconds per person at peak
One-off event or the first instance of a reusable kit
Success measures and the post-event attendance deliverable (format, recipients, sponsor access)
Who may override a refusal, add walk-ins and see attendee data, and the retention period after the event
